long-transaction.title: One open transaction stops the cleanup
long-transaction.alt: A recorded run on PostgreSQL. Session A opens a repeatable read transaction and reads. Session B updates every row and vacuums, but vacuum can't remove the old versions, because session A might still need them. After session A commits, vacuum removes them.

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ

steps.note: Another session updates every row. Each row now has an old version that A's snapshot can still see.
VACUUM can't remove them. The tag only says VACUUM, but the next step shows the result.

steps.sql: SELECT n_dead_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 't'
steps.note: All 1,000 dead versions are still there.
Now nothing needs the old versions.

write-amp.title: WAL written to update 50,000 rows
write-amp.alt: Megabytes of write-ahead log written to update 50,000 rows, as a table gains secondary indexes from none to five. Updating a column with no index stays flat, because of heap-only tuples. Updating an indexed column grows with every index on the table, even indexes on other columns.

steps.label: A new row
steps.caption: One row version, and one index entry pointing at line pointer 1.

steps.label: HOT update
steps.caption: note isn't indexed and the page has room, so the new version is heap-only. The index still has one entry, pointing at line pointer 1, and the old version links to the new one.

steps.label: HOT again
steps.caption: The chain grows, and the index still isn't touched.

steps.label: Update an indexed column
steps.caption: With an index on v, changing v can't be HOT. The new version gets its own line pointer, and every index gets a new entry, including the primary key, though id never changed.

steps.label: VACUUM
steps.caption: Dead versions are removed and the stale index entry goes with them.

hot.hint: n_tup_hot_upd counts updates that touched no index. Update the unindexed column, then the indexed one, and compare.

nulls.title: NULL isn't a value
nulls.hint: Each preset is a real trap. Try to predict the result first.
nulls.setup:
CREATE TABLE t (id int, parent int);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, NULL), (2, 1), (3, 1);

presets.label: = NULL
presets.sql: SELECT id FROM t WHERE parent = NULL;

presets.label: NOT IN with a NULL
presets.sql: SELECT id FROM t WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT parent FROM t);

presets.label: NOT EXISTS instead
presets.sql: SELECT id FROM t a WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t b WHERE b.parent = a.id);
